newsitem.title: USA: Tennessee avoids deficit, has $2 million surplus.
newsitem.headline: Tennessee avoids deficit, has $2 million surplus.

text.p: Tennessee finished fiscal 1997 with a $2 million surplus rather than the revenue shortfall previously projected.
But economic growth remains in a holding pattern, Matthew Murray, associate director of the University of Tennessee's Center for Business and Research said.

Last year, Finance Commissioner John Ferguson projected a state funding shortfall of up to $110 million for the fiscal year that ended June 30. The State Funding Board trimmed back its revenue projections for the $14.4 billion budget.
"We were very concerned earlier in the year that revenue growth was going to slow. At least based on our revised expectations we were able to close the year out with a small surplus," Murray said.

Higher sales tax collections helped ease the crunch. Collections of sales taxes, which account for 57 cents of every state tax dollar, rose 4.8 percent in July, compared to July of last year. July collections are based on June spending.
For the year, sales taxes were 6.3 percent higher.
But collections are not growing as fast as they were earlier in the decade, when the average was a robust 10 percent. For the past 18 months, growth has hovered around 5 percent, Murray said.
"I think it's good that it's holding its own but I don't see the sales tax getting stronger. I don't see an upside for the economy but there's no clear downside on the horizon either," Murray said.
The slowdown is partly an offshoot of decelerating growth in the national economy. But the state also reched full employment before the other states, Murray said.
Without new jobs to generate increased spending, tax collections fell.
"If you look at the economy over the past several years, Tennessee matured faster so that took some of the upside off," Murray said.
